A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MSA research despite the changed title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable. Revised experimental settings can be distinguished from retained content.

before.justification: V1 reports original TOFU and RESTOR experiments, checkpoint-distance evaluations, ablations, and a manual validation of its GPT-4o judge.

after.justification: V2 reports original TOFU, RESTOR, and MUSE-Books results, including experiments on repeated exposure, subsequent training, and checkpoint-augmented baselines.

M1.justification: The core MSA procedure—subtracting a checkpoint-derived forget vector and optionally adding a retain vector—is unchanged. Appendix H introduces a limited procedural adaptation for baselines: perform unlearning at an earlier checkpoint, then transfer its scaled parameter update to the target model.

E1.justification: V2 adds MUSE-Books document unlearning and TOFU scenarios involving subsequent C4 training and repeated exposure to forget data. Conversely, v1's combined TOFU-to-RESTOR experiment assessing collateral damage to TOFU knowledge is replaced by RESTOR-only evaluation. These substantially change the domains and training-history scenarios tested.

E2.justification: TOFU comparisons add SatImp and UNDIAL; the Llama-3.1-8B comparison also adds RMU and GradDiff beyond v1's NPO comparison. RMU is omitted from the corresponding 1B forget01 table. Appendix H adds checkpoint-augmented comparators. Task Vector corresponds to v1's final-checkpoint MSA variant, so that name alone does not establish a new baseline.

E3.justification: V2 changes standard TOFU training to five epochs, replaces validation on 10% of forget questions with a 15%/85% validation/test split, and selects configurations using a multi-metric score instead of Forget Quality. Searches are expanded, OLMo-2-1B is replaced by OLMo-2-7B, forget05 and Extraction Strength are added, and retain-set ROUGE is dropped. New MUSE and temporal-exposure experiments introduce additional protocols.

E4.justification: Appendices F-H newly test continued training after target exposure, repeated target exposure, and whether competing algorithms benefit from historical checkpoints. Checkpoint-distance analysis extends across benchmarks. V1's explicit TOFU no-retain-vector comparisons, longer-training ablation, and parameter-sensitivity plots are removed. The 200-example judge validation is retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or error bars. Forget Quality p-values remain in v2's appendix, and both versions report the same 200-judgment check with 96% agreement. No new uncertainty-estimation practice is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 replaces substantial TOFU and RESTOR results and adds MUSE and temporal-exposure findings. For Llama-3.1-8B forget10, MSAinstruct recovery/retention changes from 0.43/0.97 in v1 Table 9 to 0.46/0.91 in v2 Table 2. Training and selection settings differ, so these are revised results rather than a demonstrated same-setting improvement.

T1.justification: V2 introduces nonstandard mathematical definitions of composite validation scores in Appendices C.3 and E. The core MSA equations remain unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. The printed MUSE score includes (1−KnowMem_r)^2, which conflicts with its stated higher-is-better retention objective.

C1.justification: The central checkpoint-based unlearning and ideal-model-recovery claims remain. V2 qualifies blanket superiority as competitive performance with frequent improvements, narrows the highlighted checkpoint-gap claim from trillions to hundreds of billions of tokens, and replaces the prominent no-retain-set contribution with claims about membership inference and privacy metrics.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of checkpoint availability, why earlier vectors may better isolate data influence, and tradeoffs between ideal-model recovery and aggressive content removal. It gives benchmark-dependent checkpoint limits, interprets repeated exposure as favoring checkpoints before first exposure, and acknowledges possible MUSE/pretraining overlap in Appendix I. These substantially expand v1's limitations and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 documents more detailed baseline search grids, MUSE vector-training recipes, and C4 exposure settings, and reports two A100 GPUs instead of four RTX A5000s. It additionally describes supplementary reproduction scripts while retaining the repository link. However, v1's selected α/β table disappears, and Appendix E inconsistently names the MUSE Llama model as Llama-3-8B versus Llama-3.1-8B in Table 9.

R1.justification: The new extended related-work appendix compares MSA with Amnesiac Unlearning, Unrolling SGD, and Rewind-to-Delete, explicitly acknowledging earlier use of previous model states for forgetting. It positions MSA through post-hoc applicability, storage and computational requirements, and LLM-scale evaluation. Additional citations support new baselines, metrics, and checkpoint-access discussions.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and substantially reorganized: v1's separate evaluation and experimental sections become an Experiments section followed by a finding-led Results and Discussion section. The introduction and benchmark descriptions are extensively rewritten, preliminaries are separated, and the appendices are reorganized. Ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with example outputs, and the earlier ROUGE example table is replaced by two illustrated figures containing different examples. Checkpoint and sensitivity plots are removed. Results tables gain percentage annotations, color highlighting, and reorganized columns, alongside new benchmark and analysis tables and a conference-style layout.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for historical-checkpoint unlearning by testing subsequent training, repeated exposure, and checkpoint-augmented competitors, addressing important gaps in v1's evaluation. Its expanded comparison with earlier trajectory-based methods also improves research positioning. MUSE adds privacy and memorization evidence beyond factual QA. These gains outweigh the removed ablations and sensitivity results, although the contradictory retention term in Appendix E leaves the MUSE model-selection procedure partly unclear.
